💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when planning our 2026 Points of View Summit, we wanted to be sure to set time aside to hear directly from our travel specialists—the behind-the-scenes experts who work tirelessly work to curate ambitious and deeply personal itineraries around the world.
  • Jim Berkeley, founder and CEO of Destinations and Adventures International, speaks on culinary moments.
  • Inspired by Hilton Head Island's rich tapestry of culinary traditions, senior features editor Megan Spurrell and editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez led a discussion on traveling for taste—from the rising interest in foraging over traditional cooking classes to the draw of substantial-name chefs contrasted with harder-to-find local gems, and the hotspots that deserve to be on our food maps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when planning our 2026 Points of View Summit, we wanted to be sure to set time aside to hear directly from our travel specialists—the behind-the-scenes experts who work tirelessly work to curate ambitious and deeply personal itineraries around the world. Spliced between compelling panels on Lowcountry heritage, summer travel trends, and the evolving appeal of all-inclusive stays, the breakouts allowed for extended discussions with Traveler editors on a range of themes. From culinary experiences inspired by Hilton Head Island's Gullah cuisine, to the evolving dynamics of multigenerational travel and a new guard of ultra-luxe globetrotters, we got the inside scoop on where travelers are going and how they're getting there.

Jim Berkeley, founder and CEO of Destinations and Adventures International, speaks on culinary moments.

Inspired by Hilton Head Island's rich tapestry of culinary traditions, senior features editor Megan Spurrell and editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez led a discussion on traveling for taste—from the rising interest in foraging over traditional cooking classes to the draw of substantial-name chefs contrasted with harder-to-find local gems, and the hotspots that deserve to be on our food maps.

According to recent reports, our specialists all agreed that travelers yearn for “authentic” food moments, though defining authenticity—and actually finding it—often becomes tricky. To Omolola Campbell, sixth-gen Gullah descendant and executive producer of Gullah short documentary The Spirit We Move With, it's about who provides the experience. “Taking a cooking class is much different than getting it from a local chef who can tell stories about why a dish means so much to this locality,” she noted, explaining how so many of South Carolina's Gullah dishes contain okra because its seeds were sown into the hair of West Africans who were brought to the South for slavery. The plant has come to represent resilience, and it's that integral context, according to her, that gives a meal its soul. “That's how you differentiate the person who really knows why they're cooking what they're cooking,” Campbell concluded.

Dana Kravis, Madison Flager, and our travel specialists explore multigenerational travel trends.

According to recent reports, when it comes to multigenerational trips, the grandchildren are choosing the destinations and the grandparents are paying—it's their way of leaving a legacy amongst those dearest to them. During a discussion led by global executive director of video Dana Kravis and commerce director Madison Flager, our travel specialists observed that, because people today tend to wait longer to have children, grandparents are older than they used to be. Travelers in their 80s and 90s are increasingly joining trips, shifting the multigenerational travel dynamic away from the traditional picture of grandparents in their 70s. To trip designers, this means there must be layers of options catering to different activity and exertion levels.

It has been revealed that many in this session agreed the most successful family trips provide opportunities for separating and coming back together. Three itinerary choices in one day are ideal, so younger folks can be out and about, with the whole family reuniting for mealtimes and perhaps an afternoon activity. Boat and yacht experiences were especially recommended as spaces where the family is forced to be together—grandkids cannot simply run off and do their own thing.

What's luxury to one traveler might seem the furthest from it to another; some long for jam-packed, once-in-a-lifetime itineraries, while others want total disconnection and the privilege to do absolutely nothing for a week. Features director Rebecca Misner and commerce writer Jessica Sulima led this breakout, as specialists debated the definition of luxury itself. “Luxury is being able to pass on meaning to kids [and] exposing families to the broader world and its cultures,” Virgi Schiffino Kennedy, managing partner at Lux Voyage, said of its intangible appeal. To Ruchi Harnal, founder of Harnal Travel, true luxury “is not about the resort or the villa but the personalization of the trip.” As for who’s spending money on trips? Thomas Robinson, MR at Dehouche, has observed that Gen Z and Millennials are more inclined to spend but want to know where that money goes. Additionally, the specialists largely agreed they’re seeing a shift away from parents taking their children on trips, and towards 30- and 40-somethings treating their parents to a vacation. In Harnal's experience, milestone birthdays and anniversaries are driving clients to book a trip.

Between rising temperatures and overtourism, our specialists discuss the factors impacting European summer destinations.

What is the impact of overtourism, price inflation, and rising temperatures on our Euro summers? Director of special projects Lale Arikoglu and commerce editor Meaghan Kenny opened the floor for our specialists. “If you’re thinking of traveling to the Dolomites, consider Switzerland instead. There’s history and beautiful scenery with fewer crowds,” Brian Dore, owner of CIU Travel, said. For the hiking curious, some added that Switzerland offers plenty of one-day hiking trails or “soft adventure” travel—three-to-four days combined with a lake or city destination. Others agreed that traveling to the Alps offers a significant advantage—higher elevations means cooler temperatures—and that Slovenia is a great alternative to Italy. To dodge the crowds, travelers might also consider Belgium, Denmark, or Norway (where ocean ships and river cruises are opening earlier in March). For families, consider Umbria (hot tip: plenty of festival and craft opportunities for kids), Austria, Ireland, or Croatia.

It has been revealed that for those who want to stick with more tried-and-tested European itineraries next summer, consider going as early as possible, for instance, in May instead of August. When it comes to traveling to France specifically, folks advised flying into Paris or Nice, then venturing out to the countryside or oft-overlooked Atlantic Coast. And our specialists could not stress it enough: Always, always check the temperatures in advance of your trip.

As discussed by Mei Zhang, chairman and founder at WildChina, during the panel on summer travel, the demand for travel to Asia is only increasing. Global features director Erin Florio and editorial assistant Kat Chen continued the conversation with travel specialists on the destinations and experiences driving this growth. For Silk Road Treasure Tours president Zulya Rajabova and her clients, it's the destinations with indispensable craft identities, such as Samarkand in Uzbekistan with its millennia-old design traditions, that make the continent so varied yet distinct. Meanwhile, Marigold Wood, travel designer at Blonde Atlas, explained that she's been recommending routes going through China, such as Yunnan's tea trails, which offer trekking and hiking opportunities. For Ethan Crowley, lead trip designer at Asia Desk Ltd, educating his travelers on navigating countries like Cambodia, beyond their most-visited landmarks, is key.

Recent findings suggest that if 2026 was the year of the fan, 2027 is ushering in even more reasons to travel for entertainment. Associate editor Charlie Hobbs and commerce writer Jessica Chapel helmed this breakout on the sporting events, music festivals, and art fairs that specialists are seeing people travel for (and the subsequent hurdles they must overcome to). From Pink at the Sphere, where access requires a Venetian hotel package to the Ryder Cup at Adare Manor, where full-house and package buyouts, high-demand events are increasingly forcing bundled purchases.

In a recent development, the specialists also highlighted how limited legal protections in the States enables extreme ticket scalping for stadium concerts and makes domestic events increasingly unaffordable. Stephanie Malakie, founder of Empress Travel Club pointed to a related challenge: With so many events and providers, travel advisors find it hard to filter the options and identify the right fit for clients. Rather than just acquiring a ticket, specialists agreed the focus should be on curating the surrounding experience or tapping into evergreen and niche experiential travel, with events like the Jets playing in London or F1 in Shanghai. Cultural milestones like Vatican City trips featuring Papal Blessings or European Christmas markets pair well with entertainment, too. To Zhang, set-jetting to filming locations also offers value, minus the headache of peak-event ticketing.

Hannah Towey co-leads the breakout session on outdoor travel.

Everyone is hiking, or so it seems. Helmed by Jamie Spain, travel bookings commerce editor, and Hannah Towey, news editor, this breakout explored nature as wellness and why it is we're increasingly longing for all things outdoorsy. However, our specialists offered a frank reality check on our dumbphone fantasies. “Guests all want to have access [to Wi-Fi] for emergency reasons at a minimum… I don’t have a single guest who wants to [fully] digital detox," Kate Doty, trip designer at Geographic Expeditions, stated. It seems that many travelers want to be disconnected until the time comes for true disconnection, and Lou Lagrange, trip consultant at Luxury Travel Advisor, added, “Even planning for national park trips, [you have to] warn them there won’t be Wi-Fi.” However, the group observed that services such as having photographers on small ships, helps reduce a traveler's dependency on their phones.

It has been revealed that there's still a real demand for glamping, as guests want access to nature but with a side of luxury. And when it comes to extreme weather events, instead of having travelers write off entire regions or countries, Doty has figured out collaborative ways to shelve them for potential future trips. In Travel Studio founder Kerri Lisa's case, it's a matter of reframing the perks of a destination and its seasons; the rainy season, for example, might be exceptionally lush and green. There's always something to be learned in welcoming a bit of playful unpredictability into our itineraries.

Industry observers note that among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

In a recent development, since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a fresh card debuted today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To quell this problem, the upcoming card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

It has been revealed that this model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t….

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most travel is extractive and passive. You show up somewhere, take photos of the same landmarks everyone else takes photos of, eat at a restaurant the guidebook recommended, and hit up some bars. You take some tours to learn about the place and, if you’re lucky, get to meet some locals on your trip. You don’t really go deep.

Even long-term travelers who talk about how they “aren’t tourists” do the same – just at a slower pace and while trying to spend less money.

It has been revealed that and there’s nothing wrong with that. That’s just the nature of travel. While we all imagine dropping into a place, befriending locals, and having this crazy time like we’re in some movies. But that doesn’t happen. Because we’re just passing through and, for the most part, locals don’t want to become friends with tourists. In fact, most locals don’t interact with tourists. 25 Best Travel Apps for 2026: The Apps We Actually Use

📅 17 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theplanetd

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We reviewed every recommendation and added new apps for AI trip planning, eSIMs, flight tracking, budgeting, and travel safety.
  • According to recent reports, after travelling to more than 130 countries, we have used travel apps for everything from finding a last-minute room and navigating a city offline to translating menus, tracking flights and staying connected without paying ridiculous roaming charges.
  • According to recent reports, for this 2026 guide, we cut through the clutter and chose the travel apps that solve real problems before and during a trip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We reviewed every recommendation and added new apps for AI trip planning, eSIMs, flight tracking, budgeting, and travel safety.

According to recent reports, after travelling to more than 130 countries, we have used travel apps for everything from finding a last-minute room and navigating a city offline to translating menus, tracking flights and staying connected without paying ridiculous roaming charges. Some apps have earned a permanent place on our phones. Others have become outdated, overpriced or unnecessary.

According to recent reports, for this 2026 guide, we cut through the clutter and chose the travel apps that solve real problems before and during a trip. You do not need to download every app on this list. Choose the ones that match your destination, travel style and the problems you are most likely to face.

The best travel apps for 2026 are Google Maps for navigation, Google Translate for language help, WhatsApp for communication, TripIt for organizing reservations, Google Flights for comparing airfare, Booking.com for hotels, Airalo or another destination-appropriate eSIM for mobile data, Uber for rides and AllTrails for hiking. Most travellers need only one or two apps from each category.

The Best Travel Apps for 2026 at a Glance.

It has been revealed that our picks are based on usefulness, ease of use, geographic coverage and whether the app solves a genuine travel problem. We have also included alternatives where the best choice depends on your destination.

Before getting into specialized apps, these are the five we would start with. They cover navigation, translation, communication, flight updates and trip organization.

Sources indicate that google Maps is still the app we use most often while travelling. It handles driving, walking and public-transit directions, lets us save hotels and restaurants, and demonstrates opening hours, recent reviews and nearby services.

Before leaving reliable Wi-Fi, download the map for your destination. Offline maps are especially useful when you land without mobile data or drive through an area with poor reception. Keep in mind that live traffic, some transit information and certain search features may not work offline.

What we like: It combines navigation, trip planning and local research in one place.

Recent findings suggest that what to know: Directions, opening hours and business listings are not always accurate. Double-check important information directly with the business.

Our verdict: Download it before almost any trip.

It has been revealed that google Translate has helped us order food, read signs and have simple conversations in places where we did not speak the language. You can type a phrase, speak into the phone or point the camera at text for an instant translation.

In a recent development, download the languages you expect to use before your trip. That gives you a useful backup when you do not have data, although online translations can be more complete.

What we like: The camera function is incredibly useful for menus, ticket machines and signs.

What to know: Translations can be awkward or wrong, especially with slang, regional phrases and complicated instructions.

Our verdict: It is one of the most useful free international travel apps.

WhatsApp is the default communication tool in many parts of the world. Hotels, tour companies, drivers and local contacts often use it instead of standard text messages.

It has been revealed that it supports individual and group chats, voice calls, video calls, photos, documents and live-location sharing over an internet connection. That makes it useful for keeping a travel group together or confirming a pickup without paying international texting charges.

What we like: It is widely used and keeps trip communication in one place.

Sources indicate that what to know: It needs mobile data or Wi-Fi. Check the phone number carefully before sharing personal information or sending money.

Our verdict: Install it before leaving home and verify your number while you can still receive regular text messages.

According to recent reports, this may not be the most exciting recommendation, but it is one of the most practical. Download your airline’s official app before departure and sign in to your booking.

It has been revealed that airline apps can provide mobile check-in, boarding passes, gate notifications, delay information and rebooking options. During a disruption, the app may update before airport screens or email notifications do.

What we like: It gives you a direct line to the airline’s current information about your flight.

It has been revealed that what to know: Push notifications are useful, but do not rely on them alone. Keep checking the departure board and listen for airport announcements.

Our verdict: Download it for every flight, even if you delete it after the trip.

TripIt turns confirmation emails into one organized itinerary. Forward your flight, hotel, rental-car and activity confirmations, and the app puts the details in chronological order.

It has been revealed that this is particularly useful on complicated trips with several flights, hotel changes or train journeys. Instead of searching through your inbox at a check-in desk, you can pull up the reservation in one place.

What we like: It reduces the chaos of juggling confirmation emails.

What to know: Review imported details because automatic parsing is not infallible. Real-time alerts are generally part of the paid plan.

Our verdict: Best for multi-stop trips, business travel and anyone who likes everything organized.

Recent findings suggest that AI can be helpful for brainstorming routes, comparing neighbourhoods, creating packing lists and turning scattered ideas into a first-draft itinerary. It should not be treated as the final authority on visa rules, border requirements, prices, opening hours, transit schedules or safety alerts. Verify anything that could cost you money or prevent you from entering a country.

ChatGPT is most useful when you give it real constraints: your travel dates, budget, interests, pace, mobility needs and where you are staying. It can then help turn those details into a practical first draft rather than a generic list of attractions.

We also use AI to compare neighbourhoods, create checklists and identify questions we still need to research. The trick is to treat the result as a planning assistant, not a booking engine or government authority.

What we like: It is flexible and can swiftly reorganize a complicated trip.

According to recent reports, what to know: AI can produce outdated or invented information. Always confirm bookings, travel rules, prices and operating hours through official sources.

Our verdict: Excellent for planning and editing; unreliable as the sole source of truth.

According to recent reports, wanderlog combines itinerary planning, maps, reservations, notes and collaboration. It is useful for road trips and group travel because several people can add places and adjust the strategy.

The visual map helps reveal when an itinerary makes no geographic sense. That sounds obvious, but it is remarkably easy to plan breakfast on one side of a city, lunch on the other and dinner back where you started.

What we like: The shared planning and map view make group trips easier.

Recent findings suggest that what to know: A detailed itinerary can become cluttered. Keep some flexibility rather than scheduling every hour.

Our verdict: A strong choice for collaborative planning and road trips.

Industry observers note that finding a cheap flight is only part of the job. These apps help us compare dates, monitor prices and track disruptions once the trip begins.

In a recent development, google Flights is not a conventional downloadable app, but it remains one of the fastest ways to compare airfare. The calendar and price graph make it easy to see whether leaving a day earlier or using a nearby airport could reduce the fare.

Set a price alert when you are not ready to book. Google Flights sends updates when fares change, but you will usually complete the purchase with the airline or another booking provider.

What we like: It is fast, flexible and excellent for comparing dates.

What to know: It does not show every airline or every possible fare. Compare the final price, baggage allowance and change rules before booking.

Sources indicate that our verdict: Our first stop for airfare research. Before pressing confirm, read our guide to airline booking traps that can make a cheap flight cost more.

Recent findings suggest that skyscanner is useful when you know you want to travel but have not settled on a destination. Its flexible search tools can surface options by month, country or broad destination.

It also compares hotels and rental cars, although we mainly use it for flight discovery. Once you find a fare, pay close attention to whether the booking is through the airline or an online travel agency.

What we like: Flexible searches are ideal for travellers who can follow the deal.

Recent findings suggest that what to know: The cheapest result is not automatically the best one. Customer service and change policies vary by booking provider.

Our verdict: Best for inspiration and flexible travel dates.

Available on: iOS and supported Apple devices.

Flighty turns a flight number into a detailed timeline with schedule changes, aircraft information and disruption updates. Frequent flyers appreciate how quickly it presents complicated flight information.

It is most useful on travel days, especially when weather or airport congestion starts knocking schedules sideways. The free version is enough for occasional travellers, while frequent flyers may value the paid alerts.

What we like: It presents flight changes clearly and can reduce airport uncertainty.

What to know: Some of its best features require a subscription, and platform availability may not suit every traveller.

Our verdict: A specialist app worth considering if you fly often.

In a recent development, finding the right place to stay is about more than price. We look at location, recent reviews, cancellation policies, hidden fees, and whether the property actually suits the way we travel. These accommodation apps make it easier to compare hotels, apartments, hostels, and vacation rentals without bouncing between a dozen websites.

Industry observers note that booking.com remains one of the easiest places to compare a wide range of accommodation, from simple guesthouses to luxury hotels. The filters are especially useful when we need parking, a specific neighbourhood, breakfast, air conditioning or a refundable rate.

Recent findings suggest that read recent reviews rather than relying only on the overall score. We pay particular attention to comments about noise, cleanliness, construction and whether the room matches the photos.

What we like: Huge inventory and practical search filters.

What to know: Cancellation and payment rules vary by property. Confirm whether taxes and resort fees are included before booking.

Our verdict: Our top general-purpose hotel app.

Airbnb is most useful when we want a kitchen, laundry, a living area or enough bedrooms for a group. It can also provide options in neighbourhoods with few conventional hotels.

Compare the total price rather than the nightly rate. Cleaning charges, service fees and local taxes can change the value swiftly. Read the house rules and cancellation policy before paying, and check whether the host has a substantial history of recent reviews.

What we like: It can provide more space and practical amenities than a hotel.

What to know: Quality is inconsistent, and fees can make a seemingly cheap stay expensive.

Our verdict: Best for longer stays and groups, not automatically the cheapest option.

Best for: Hostels, dorms, private rooms and social accommodation.

Price: Free to search; booking deposit or fees may apply.

Available on: iOS, Android and web.

Hostelworld makes it easy to compare hostels by location, room type, atmosphere and recent guest reviews. It is particularly useful for solo travellers who care about communal spaces and meeting other people.

Industry observers note that do not assume every hostel is a party hostel—or that every quiet-looking property will actually be quiet. Read recent reviews for comments about security, lockers, bathrooms, noise and the surrounding area.

What we like: It provides hostel-specific details that general hotel sites often miss.

In a recent development, what to know: A low bed price can rise after taxes, linen fees or deposits. Check whether lockers require your own padlock.

Our verdict: The most useful specialist app for hostel travellers.

According to recent reports, there is no single eSIM provider that is cheapest or fastest in every country. Compare the local network, amount of high-speed data, hotspot rules, validity period and whether the strategy is data-only before buying.

Airalo makes it straightforward to buy and install an eSIM before a trip. You choose the destination, select a data package and follow the installation instructions on a compatible phone.

We like that it removes the need to find a physical SIM card immediately after landing. Regional looks can also be convenient on multi-country trips, although a country-specific proposal may offer better value.

What we like: Easy setup and broad destination coverage.

What to know: Most aims are data-only, and the local network or speed can vary. Check phone compatibility before purchasing.

Our verdict: A convenient starting point for travellers fresh to eSIMs.

Sources indicate that ubigi is worth comparing with Airalo because eSIM value changes by country. In some destinations, one provider may offer a better local carrier, more data or a longer validity period.

In a recent development, install the app and eSIM before departure whenever possible. Take screenshots of the setup instructions in case your connection disappears halfway through activation.

What we like: It gives travellers another established option instead of assuming one provider always wins.

Industry observers note that what to know: Coverage and value depend on the specific strategy. Read the plan details rather than buying based only on the headline price.

Our verdict: Compare it destination by destination.

Recent findings suggest that getting around an unfamiliar city can be one of the most confusing parts of travel. These apps help us compare public transit, initiative longer connections, and arrange rides when trains or buses are not practical.

Citymapper can be easier to understand than a standard map when a city has several transit systems layered on top of one another. It compares routes, indicates transfers and often gives useful instructions about which station exit to use.

We find it particularly useful in large cities where choosing the wrong train direction or exit can add a surprising amount of time.

What we like: Clear transit directions and route comparisons.

What to know: Coverage is limited to supported cities, and live information depends on local transit data.

Our verdict: Excellent in cities where it is available.

It has been revealed that rome2Rio is useful during the early planning stage when you know where you want to go but not how to get there. Enter two places and it outlines possible combinations of flights, trains, buses, ferries and driving routes.

We use it as a starting point rather than the final booking authority. Once we understand the route, we verify schedules and buy tickets directly from the transport operator whenever practical.

What we like: It makes complicated overland connections easier to visualize.

What to know: Estimated times and prices can change. Confirm every important connection with the operator.

Our verdict: One of the best tools for answering, ‘How do we actually get there?’.

Uber can remove the uncertainty of explaining a destination, handling cash and negotiating a fare in an unfamiliar city. The app shows the route, vehicle and driver details before the ride begins.

Availability and regulations vary widely. In some destinations, another local app is more common, and airports may require pickup from a designated ride-hailing area.

What we like: Upfront trip details and cashless payment are convenient.

It has been revealed that what to know: Surge pricing can be expensive. Always confirm the licence plate and driver before getting into a vehicle.

Our verdict: Useful where it operates, but check the dominant local alternative.

In a recent development, managing money abroad can get complicated rapidly. Exchange rates, foreign transaction fees, ATM charges, and shared expenses all add up, especially on longer trips or when travelling with other people. These apps help us understand what things really cost, manage different currencies, and keep track of who paid for what without turning dinner into an accounting meeting.

Wise lets eligible customers hold and exchange several currencies and spend with a linked card. It can be useful for frequent travellers, remote workers and anyone receiving money in more than one currency.

Always compare the total conversion cost with your regular bank or credit card. The best option depends on your country, card benefits and the type of transaction.

What we like: Transparent conversion information and multi-currency tools.

In a recent development, what to know: Availability, card features and fees vary by country. It is a financial service, so protect the account with strong security.

Our verdict: A useful tool for frequent international travellers.

XE is the app we open when a price full of unfamiliar zeros makes our brains quietly leave the room. It converts currencies rapidly and helps you understand what a meal, taxi or hotel actually costs in your home currency.

Remember that the rate shown in a converter is not necessarily the rate your bank, ATM or exchange desk will give you after fees.

What we like: Fast, simple conversions.

What to know: It reveals a reference rate, not a guaranteed retail exchange rate.

Our verdict: Keep it on your phone for quick price checks.

Sources indicate that splitwise prevents the end-of-trip ritual where everyone stares at a pile of receipts and suddenly forgets who paid for the rental car. Add shared expenses as you go, assign who owes what and let the app calculate the running balance.

It is particularly helpful for groups using different payment methods or taking turns covering major expenses.

What we like: It reduces awkward money conversations and messy arithmetic.

Recent findings suggest that what to know: It records debts but does not automatically settle every balance. Agree on currencies and exchange rates at the beginning of the trip.

Our verdict: Essential for group trips.

Recent findings suggest that booking tours and activities in advance can save time, especially when popular attractions have timed entry or limited availability. We use these apps to compare tours, skip-the-line tickets, day trips, and local experiences, but we always check the operator, recent reviews, cancellation policy, and exactly what is included before booking.

GetYourGuide is useful when timed-entry tickets sell out or when a guided visit adds real context. It covers major attractions, walking tours, food tours, day trips and airport transfers in many popular destinations.

Read the cancellation policy and identify the actual tour operator before booking. A marketplace can list several versions of what looks like the same experience.

What we like: Strong inventory in major tourism destinations.

What to know: Quality depends on the local operator, not only the booking platform.

Our verdict: A good place to compare organized experiences.

Viator has a broad inventory of tours and activities around the world. We use it to see what is available, compare departure times and identify experiences that may be difficult to organize independently.

Sources indicate that as with any marketplace, read the newest reviews and check exactly what is included. A low starting price may refer to a basic option without transport, admission or the advertised upgrade.

What we like: It covers an enormous range of destinations and activities.

Sources indicate that what to know: Listings from different operators can look very similar. Check inclusions, pickup details and cancellation terms.

Our verdict: Best for comparing a wide range of tours.

According to recent reports, finding the right trail or campsite takes more than choosing the prettiest photo. We look at distance, difficulty, recent trail conditions, offline map access, weather, and whether the route matches our experience level. These hiking, camping, and outdoor apps help us initiative more confidently, but they should always be used alongside proper preparation and local safety information.

Recent findings suggest that allTrails is an easy starting point for finding hikes by location, distance, difficulty and user rating. Recent reviews can reveal muddy sections, closures, parking problems and trail conditions that a static guidebook cannot.

Sources indicate that download the route before leaving reception and carry a backup. A phone app is useful, but it does not replace proper preparation, weather awareness or a dedicated navigation tool in remote terrain.

What we like: It makes trail discovery accessible and provides recent user feedback.

What to know: Crowdsourced routes can be inaccurate. Do not rely on a single phone app for serious backcountry navigation.

Our verdict: Best for day hikes and casual outdoor planning.

Industry observers note that gaia GPS is aimed at travellers who need more detail than a simple trail list. It supports topographic maps, route planning and map layers useful for hiking, camping and remote travel.

Learn how to use it before heading into the backcountry. Download the required maps, carry power and tell someone your route. Technology is helpful right up until the battery dies.

What we like: Detailed mapping and route-planning tools.

What to know: It has a learning curve, and key map features may require a subscription.

Our verdict: Better suited to experienced outdoor travellers than casual city walkers.

The following apps can be excellent, but they are more specialized or depend heavily on your destination:.

Hidden-city ticketing involves booking a connecting itinerary and intentionally leaving at the connection instead of taking the final flight. It can violate airline conditions, makes checked baggage impractical and can cause the rest of an itinerary to be cancelled. We would not build a trip around it.

In a recent development, price forecasts can be useful signals, but airfare and hotel prices remain unpredictable. Treat predictions as estimates, not promises. Book when the price, schedule and cancellation terms work for your trip.

Recent findings suggest that use apps to organize information, not to replace official immigration sources. Entry requirements can depend on nationality, residency, passport type, trip purpose and even transit airports.

Sources indicate that google Maps can provide offline driving navigation for downloaded areas, and Google Translate supports downloaded language packs. Outdoor apps such as AllTrails and Gaia GPS can offer offline maps depending on the plan. Save boarding passes, hotel addresses and reservation numbers before leaving Wi-Fi.

AI can build a useful first draft, but it should not be allowed to quietly invent your holiday. Use it to organize ideas, compare possible routes and identify questions. Then verify flights, hotels, opening hours, ticket rules, visa requirements and safety information through official or first-party sources.

It has been revealed that an eSIM can be useful when your regular carrier charges high roaming fees. Compare the local network, data allowance, hotspot rules and validity period before purchasing.

Which travel apps work without internet?

Google Maps and Google Translate support downloaded offline content. Some hiking apps provide offline maps through paid plans. Download everything before leaving reliable Wi-Fi.

The best travel app is not the one with the longest feature list. It is the one that solves a problem at the moment you need it. For us, Google Maps, Google Translate, WhatsApp, an airline app and an itinerary organizer cover the basics. From there, we add an eSIM, flight tracker, budgeting app or hiking map depending on the trip.

Download your essentials before leaving home, test that you can sign in and save critical information offline. Then put the phone away once in a while. The app is supposed to help you experience the trip—not become the trip.

In a recent development, theater legend Audra McDonald possesses one of the most powerful, lauded voices of her generation, a soprano so stunning that she’s been nominated for more Tony Awards than any other performer in history. So what elixirs, potions, and special teas does she keep with her to ensure the quality of her voice as she travels the world to sing? “I mask up on planes. I’m traveling all over the country to do concerts; I can’t land and be sick,” she states. “And I try to make sure there's a humidifier in the hotel room. Those are the two main things.”.

While her role in the period drama The Gilded Age doesn’t require singing—yet!—McDonald and the many Broadway legends in the cast released a holiday album this month, ‘Voices of the Gilded Age: The Christmas Album,’ and the fourth season is presently airing on HBO. She spoke with Condé Nast Traveler from Australia, where her husband Will Swenson is currently starring in the Oz production of A Beautiful Noise: The Neil Diamond Musical, about traveling with their 10-year-old daughter, the unspeakable glories of Upcoming Zealand, and why you simply can’t top New York City in the final months of the year.

The world’s best city for the holidays:.

I don't think you can beat Fresh York City. I've lived there for 36 years and it's always such a beautiful time. We have dear friends with a kid around my youngest child's age, and we've been going to the holiday spectacular at Radio City. My sister makes sure that she takes my daughters to The Nutcracker every year at City Ballet. We always try to go see the tree at Rockefeller Center. The one day I don't like in New York City during the holidays is Santa Con, but other than that, I'm down.

Her favorite venue on Earth in which to perform:.

There's something about Carnegie Hall [in Manhattan] that is magic. I last sang at Carnegie Hall about six, seven months ago—I'm on the board there now, as well—and the nerves I normally get [before a performance] are always tenfold when I'm getting ready there.

Sources indicate that then the minute I step out on that stage, the hall just gives you a hug that states, You're here to do what you're supposed to do. You're supposed to make music, you're supposed to celebrate music, you're supposed to commune with your audience, and glorious sounds are supposed to be heard. Carnegie Hall is built for all the sound to be glorious. That [venue] takes care of me.

Her advice for traveling with kids:.

Don't worry about how they act up on a plane. Do what you can, but it's not the flight attendants’ first time at the rodeo. You're never going to see any of these other people again. When we flew out to Australia, my daughter got some weird stomach bug that started the minute they shut the door, and she vomited for the first eight hours of that 15-hour flight. The flight attendants just kept bringing bags and stuff and were like… [mimes a blasé hand gesture]. There was nothing we could do! We were over the ocean. I was giving myself grace. I was giving my poor daughter grace. I just wanted her to feel better, and I was doing the best I could. That’s what I would say to other parents. They’ve seen it all, so don’t worry about what other people are thinking. Everybody has headphones now! We’re fine!

How she spends her flight time:.

It has been revealed that I am not preparing for work! That's the ADHD in me. I am also not sleeping because I cannot sleep on planes very well, unless I'm really knocked out with the help of sleeping pills or something, and I don't like to do that. I try to watch movies, but I'm not good at it, either. My dad was killed in a plane crash about 20 years ago, so normally what I'm doing on a plane—when I'm not taking care of my daughter vomiting—is watching the flight path and seeing where we are in the sky. Then, if there's Wi-Fi, I check to see the weather ahead. Like I'm helping! I don't know what I'm doing, but it calms me down to be like, “Okay, I see that there is weather up ahead, so I should expect that it's probably going to be bumpy.” I don't know if in my mind, I'm thinking [as if] I can warn the pilot. I’ve got to go to therapy, but that's what I do on a plane.

The best vacation she’s ever taken:.

Fresh Zealand, holy wow. My husband and I were asked to sing on a Playbill cruise in Tahiti. We flew to Tahiti with our two daughters, and then I had three and a half weeks off before I started my Australian tour, so we went to New Zealand. I'm going to get emotional talking about it. Every place we visited—the North Island, the South Island, Queenstown, Rotorua, Hahei Beach, the Southern Alps, Christchurch, Wellington—all of it was just one wow after another. The people were lovely. We went to Hobbiton. We drove everywhere, and every second of it was mind-blowing. We even did the mailboat, where you go with this guy on a boat to deliver the mail in an area you can only access by water. I want to go back!

The destination she swears she loved before everyone else:.

In a recent development, when we first start going, I wasn’t hearing about a lot of people there, but now everybody goes to Portugal. We have friends who live there, so we started visiting a lot, and not just Lisbon or the Algarve or Porto, though we love Porto. It was also the beautiful countryside and hills and tiny little villages. The topography there is stunning. It’s getting more expensive now, but we used to get incredible bottles of wine for €3! In fact, we have a farm there now, we love it so much.

The hotel amenity she always checks for:.

In a recent development, toothbrush and toothpaste. Not every hotel provides that, and I just love it when they do. If they've got a toothbrush and toothpaste in there, they've probably gotten a lot of the other amenities right too.

The farthest flung place she’s ever been recognized:.

Here in Australia. I was in the South Melbourne neighborhood we've been living in, and I went into a little bookstore near my daughter's school, and someone recognized me. They said, “Were you the one who recorded Emily Wilson's translation of The Iliad book on tape? I loved your work in that.” And I was like, “Whoa, what? Yes I did, wow, thank you.” Doing The Iliad on tape almost killed me. It was the hardest thing I've ever done, so the fact that she wanted to thank me for it? I don’t think my mom knows I did that!

Recent findings suggest that I really want to take a trip to Africa. Obviously, I want to go to Ghana and see where our journey started. I want to go to Kenya and do a safari. I want to go on a trek to see the gorillas. I've been to Egypt, to Cairo, but that's the only time I've been to Africa. I want to wait a couple more years, until my daughter's about 13, and then I will take her. That's going to be our trip.

Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that president Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug.
  • Sources indicate that in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir.
  • Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that president Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his latest memoir, Biden said he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Sources indicate that in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s upcoming book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major complications of our time.

It’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

Recent findings suggest that the sheer length of his newly introduced book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

It has been revealed that supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single concern in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most vital foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”.

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

It has been revealed that “We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he claims. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”.

According to recent reports, one of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”.

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

“I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling highlighted only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”.

“I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden notes. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have noted it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”.

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

“I had it on good authority that several major names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

📅 16 May 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Godsavethepoints

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for Newly introduced York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots.
  • In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies.
  • In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for Newly introduced York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

According to recent reports, the whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

Sources indicate that the fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

In a recent development, let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following….

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter organization which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have….

Sources indicate that travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

Industry observers note that I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

In a recent development, their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

Sources indicate that the app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

Recent findings suggest that all the great, major airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

In a recent development, tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

Sources indicate that if Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

According to recent reports, let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and tech giant books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so significant time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

According to recent reports, I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

According to recent reports, I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

According to recent reports, my only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

Sources indicate that so yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or fresh seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a latest golden age, again.

#19728. How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

📅 23 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1558 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nomadicmatt ↗ Open Full Page

How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

📅 23 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, drones are huge.
  • There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1.
  • I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

Sources indicate that what make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

Sources indicate that the sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

It has been revealed that most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

Recent findings suggest that and the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

The Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

The drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most customers will likely never switch back.

Here’s a video of the drone in action:.

According to recent reports, the marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

The color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

Recent findings suggest that the “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

While 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

Industry observers note that in terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

Sources indicate that the Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

Sources indicate that while the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.
