    Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
    • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
    • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    Industry observers note that hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    Recent findings suggest that that bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”.

    Industry observers note that “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley mentioned. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very tech giant that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox remarked in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    “We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    Recent findings suggest that “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles noted. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

    #19637. Tech Report: Why Delta Air Lines' Brand-Upcoming Airbus A321neos Sat In The Desert While Flying 44 Recliners Instead

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1853 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Why Delta Air Lines' Brand-Upcoming Airbus A321neos Sat In The Desert While Flying 44 Recliners Instead

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, when airlines order a upcoming fleet of aircraft, the assumption is usually straightforward - the aircraft arrive from the manufacturer, crews are trained, routes are assigned, and passengers begin flying on them shortly afterward.
    • According to recent reports, the story is not really about a dispute between an airline and a seat manufacturer.
    • Delta's A321neo premium transcontinental program was supposed to represent a major step forward in the airline's domestic premium offering.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, when airlines order a upcoming fleet of aircraft, the assumption is usually straightforward - the aircraft arrive from the manufacturer, crews are trained, routes are assigned, and passengers begin flying on them shortly afterward. Yet Delta Air Lines' newest Airbus A321neos have become an unusual example of how a single component can disrupt an entire fleet strategy. Rather than entering service with the premium cabins they were designed to showcase, several of the airline's newest narrowbody aircraft spent months sitting in desert storage while the carrier searched for a way to make them operational.

    According to recent reports, the story is not really about a dispute between an airline and a seat manufacturer. Instead, it is a case study in how modern airline products have become so specialized that a single certification delay can ripple through fleet planning, network strategy, customer experience, and competitive positioning. In the case of Delta, the issue became so severe that the airline ultimately introduced a temporary cabin featuring 44 domestic first class recliner seats on aircraft originally intended to offer one of the most advanced premium transcontinental products in the US.

    Delta's A321neo premium transcontinental program was supposed to represent a major step forward in the airline's domestic premium offering. The aircraft were expected to operate some of the carrier's most key routes, particularly those linking major coastal business markets where travelers increasingly expect an experience that rivals international business class, such as New York John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    At the center of the strategy was the Safran Vue business class seat. Unlike traditional herringbone layouts that angle passengers toward the aisle, the Vue featured a reverse-herringbone design that positioned passengers toward the window. The concept promised privacy, comfort, and views, giving the SkyTeam carrier a product that looked noticeably different from what competitors were offering.

    According to recent reports, the planned cabin reflected that premium focus, with each aircraft featuring 16 lie-flat business class suites, 12 premium economy seats, 54 Comfort+ seats, and 66 economy class seats. The layout balanced high-yield premium demand with the practical need to carry a substantial number of leisure travelers.

    That strategy was hardly surprising, given that premium transcontinental travel has become one of the most competitive segments of the US airline industry. Travelers flying between markets such as New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Boston, and Seattle increasingly expect direct aisle access, lie-flat seating, upgraded dining, and enhanced privacy. Airlines have responded by investing heavily in premium cabins, often treating them as key differentiators. For Delta, the Safran Vue was more than just another seat. It was intended to become a signature product that would reinforce the airline's premium positioning while helping it stand out from products such as JetBlue Airways' Mint and American Airlines' Flagship Suite.

    Reports emerging throughout 2025 and 2026 pointed toward persistent certification challenges involving the Safran Vue seat. While passengers often focus on comfort, privacy, and aesthetics, every airline seat must also satisfy extensive safety requirements before regulators allow it to enter commercial service.

    Industry observers note that the reported complications centered on certification standards set by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), including human factors testing and crashworthiness requirements. These standards are designed to ensure that passengers can evacuate safely, move through the cabin efficiently, and remain protected during emergency situations. Even seemingly small changes to a seat's geometry can trigger extensive review processes.

    Industry observers have suggested that the difficulties expose a broader challenge facing the airline interiors sector, and over the past decade, premium airline seats have become increasingly complex. Features such as privacy doors, large entertainment screens, charging systems, storage compartments, and customized shell designs have transformed business class seats into highly sophisticated products, while regulators remain focused on ensuring safety standards are maintained regardless of how innovative a design may be. That can create tension between manufacturers seeking differentiation and regulators seeking consistency.

    The Safran Vue was not simply another variation of an existing product - its reverse-herringbone layout represented a notable departure from more conventional designs. Every departure from established layouts can generate additional questions during certification, particularly when passenger movement and evacuation procedures are involved.

    For Delta, the result was a growing disconnect between aircraft deliveries and cabin readiness. The airline's fleet strategy assumed the premium product would be available when the aircraft arrived, but instead, aircraft began arriving while the seat certification process remained unresolved.

    Sources indicate that perhaps the most remarkable aspect is that Delta had already accepted delivery of several A321neos during 2024. Under normal circumstances, taking delivery marks the start of an aircraft's operational life, and airlines spend billions on fleet renewal programs because they expect those assets to begin generating revenue as promptly as possible.

    Industry observers note that without certified seats, however, the aircraft could not enter service in the originally intended form. Delta therefore faced a difficult decision - it could continue waiting indefinitely for certification progress, or it could temporarily remove the aircraft from active planning until a solution emerged. The result was the unusual sight of factory-fresh Airbus A321neos sitting in desert storage, with such facilities more commonly associated with retired aircraft, seasonal fleet adjustments, or aircraft awaiting resale.

    Sources indicate that the situation demonstrated how dependent modern airline programs can become on individual suppliers. Airbus had delivered the aircraft, pilots and flight attendants could be trained, and routes could be scheduled, yet a single unresolved component prevented the intended product from entering service. There were also significant financial implications. While airlines rarely pay published list prices, an Airbus A321neo still represents a major investment, and every month spent parked in storage reduced utilization and delayed revenue that those aircraft were expected to generate.

    Beyond the direct financial impact, the delays complicated broader fleet planning. Airlines carefully coordinate aircraft deliveries with staffing, maintenance schedules, route releases, and network growth initiatives. When newly delivered aircraft suddenly become unavailable, those plans often require adjustment, turning what was once a seat certification challenge into a broader operational issue.

    It has been revealed that faced with ongoing uncertainty, Delta eventually opted for a practical workaround. Rather than waiting indefinitely for the intended lie-flat business class suites, the airline developed a temporary cabin configuration that would allow the aircraft to begin carrying passengers. Introduced in May, the interim layout transformed the aircraft into something unlike any other narrowbody currently flying for the carrier. Instead of the planned mix of business class suites and premium economy seating, the aircraft received a large domestic first class cabin featuring 44 recliner seats.

    Industry observers note that the complete configuration consists of 44 first class seats, 54 Comfort+ seats, and 66 economy class seats. Compared with the original design, the temporary layout dramatically increases the number of premium seats while eliminating the lie-flat product that was supposed to define the aircraft. In effect, Delta created an aircraft that remains heavily weighted toward premium travelers while avoiding the certification complications associated with the original seats. From an operational standpoint, the decision makes sense, as aircraft create value when they are flying, not when they are parked in storage. By introducing a temporary configuration, Delta could finally deploy the aircraft across its network and begin generating revenue from them.

    Recent findings suggest that the move also demonstrates the airline's desire to maintain momentum. Waiting years for certification complications to be resolved would have left valuable aircraft sitting idle, so while the interim product differs significantly from the original vision, it lets Delta use the fleet while longer-term decisions are made. At the same time, every flight operated with 44 recliners instead of lie-flat suites serves as a reminder of how different the final product may have been had the original plan proceeded on schedule.

    Industry observers note that the temporary cabin solved one major challenge, but it also created several unusual operational quirks, including lavatory access within the enlarged first class cabin. With 44 premium passengers seated at the front of the aircraft and only a single forward lavatory, the passenger-to-bathroom ratio is unusually high for a premium-heavy cabin where convenience is typically emphasized.

    Recent findings suggest that on longer Transcontinental routes, the arrangement could create queues that passengers would not normally associate with a premium experience. One traditional advantage of premium cabins is reduced competition for onboard facilities. The temporary layout partially undermines that benefit simply because of the unusually large number of first class seats.

    It has been revealed that the customer experience also differs considerably from what Delta originally intended. The carrier's domestic first class recliner seats remain comfortable, particularly on shorter flights, but they fall into a different category than private lie-flat suites. Travelers expecting a cutting-edge premium cabin may instead get a more traditional domestic experience.

    Crew operations are also affected, as boarding procedures, meal service, and passenger interactions all change when 44 passengers occupy the premium cabin. While none of these challenges are insurmountable, they create a unique operating environment compared with the airline's original plans, and in many ways, the lavatory issue has become symbolic of the broader situation - it highlights how an airline can end up making unexpected compromises when a key component of its long-term strategy fails to arrive on schedule.

    Sources indicate that the biggest question now concerns the program's future. Reports suggest Delta may be considering abandoning the Safran Vue altogether and adopting the Thompson Vantage Solo seat instead. Such a move would represent more than a simple supplier change. The Thompson Vantage Solo is already used by airlines, including JetBlue and American Airlines, and follows a more conventional aisle-facing herringbone layout; while potentially easier to certify, it would eliminate one of the key differentiators that Delta originally hoped to bring to market.

    From a practical perspective, switching to a proven product could reduce uncertainty and accelerate deployment. Airlines generally prefer predictable solutions when schedules, fleet looks, and customer expectations are involved, and a seat with an established certification history may appear increasingly attractive after years of delays. There would also be strategic consequences, as the window-facing reverse-herringbone concept was intended to provide a unique selling point. Replacing it with a more conventional product would therefore narrow the distinction between Delta and its competitors in the premium transcontinental market.

    Meanwhile, competitors continue investing in their own premium products. JetBlue Mint remains a strong force in premium transcontinental markets, while American Airlines continues rolling out newer Flagship Suite concepts. Against that backdrop, delays to the Airbus A321neo premium program also influence how Delta positions itself within one of the industry's most competitive markets.

    Industry observers note that whether Delta ultimately waits for the Safran Vue, adopts the Thompson Vantage Solo, or pursues another alternative entirely, the episode has already become a fascinating example of how modern airline strategies can hinge on remarkably specific details. A single seat design intended to create a competitive advantage instead delayed a flagship product, sent brand-latest aircraft into desert storage, and forced Delta to fly one of the most unusual premium cabin configurations currently operating in the US.

    #19635. Latest Update: Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1008 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s fresh ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s fresh ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

    The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., stated, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

    Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five newly introduced air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

    They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

    But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

    Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

    “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

    Still, Cruz remarked the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

    Industry observers note that senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz noted that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

    Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

    Recent findings suggest that for his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., mentioned the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

    Sources indicate that “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott noted, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”.

    Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

    “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

    It has been revealed that he called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

    Industry observers note that “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy noted. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

    Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he remarked that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

    A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

    It has been revealed that the telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

    Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

    The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

    Sources indicate that bedford stated he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

    David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television demonstrates, and more. This time, we take a look at The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

    Sources indicate that we’re heading back to Panem for the sixth time this autumn, as the latest Hunger Games prequel hits screens. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the action of the first film and tells the origin story of Katniss Everdeen’s grumpy tutor, Haymitch Abernathy, as he enters the Games himself.

    Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy and Whitney Peak as Lenore Dove Baird.

    Based on the books by Suzanne Collins, the dystopian series is set in a futuristic America in which each district must send a teenage tribute to fight to the death in an annual competition—the idea being that, by doing so, the public will be too afraid to rebel against President Snow.

    In a recent development, this edition of the games is known as the Quarter Quell, with double the number of tributes being sent into the arena, meaning the stakes are so much higher. Interest in the film is high, not least because Haymitch is so beloved in the original series, portrayed by Woody Harrelson. Newcomer Joseph Zada takes the lead role in the latest film, while Hollywood heavyweights Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Elle Fanning, and Kieran Culkin also star.

    One of the most important sets in the film is the arena where the games take place, and for this, director Francis Lawrence opted not for CGI and a green screen, but instead a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in northern Spain. Below, we look into the locations used in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

    Ben Wang as Wyatt Callow, Percy Daggs IV as Ampert Latier, Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy, and Mckenna Grace as Maysilee Donner in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

    It has been revealed that within the book and film series, the settings for the Hunger Games are always known to be virtually spectacular. For this film, filmmakers settled on the vast and untouched landscape of Somiedo Natural Park in the Asturias region of northern Spain, which boasts mountain ranges, glacial valleys, beautiful meadows, dense forests, and tranquil lakes. The remote region is also home to the last brown bear population in Europe.

    When the tributes are rolled out into the arena, they are presented with a vast Cornucopia, a pile of weapons, food, and other supplies that might be useful to them in the competition. These scenes were filmed at Somiedo Natural Park, with the Asturian mountains and a glacial lake in the background.

    “Somiedo is a spectacular place,” said Pedro Aráez, supervising location manager. “The valleys, forests, and mountains have a very wild, untouched feeling, which was exactly what the filmmakers were looking for. It’s remote, dramatic, and visually unique. When you arrive there, you immediately understand why it was chosen.”.

    According to recent reports, located close to Somiedo, the Teverga beech forest, Hayedo de Montegrande, was used for some of the dense woodland scenes, in which contestants battle it out and hide in the woods. Other scenes filmed here utilized a series of glacial lakes, the Saliencia Lakes and the Lago de la Cueva.

    Iris Apatow as Proserpina Trinket and Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

    Before the tributes are launched into the arena, they are first held in special little pods underground which are arranged in a circle around the Cornucopia. The perfect location for this? A velodrome, of course, which is steeply circular so cyclists can race around it. The film crew utilized Berlin’s Velodrom for this very purpose, with its cold, clinical silver decor perfect for matching the hi-tech aesthetic associated with the Capitol.

    Ralph Fiennes as President Snow.

    Recent findings suggest that prior to entering the Games, tributes must introduce themselves on the public stage, during a televised grand chariot parade in the Capitol. Another Berlin location with links to the sporting world was used for this purpose: the Olympiastadion. For fans of the earlier films, this is the moment when Jennifer Lawrence’s character Katniss becomes “the girl on fire” with her incredible flaming dress.

    It has been revealed that the futuristic architecture of Edificio Calatrava in Oviedo, Spain—with its striking, claw-like structure—stands in for a building in the Capitol, where President Snow and his government live. The complex was designed by Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava, whose work is known for resembling living organisms. Meanwhile, the 14th-century Ehreshoven Castle, just outside of Cologne, was also used as a filming location, with local press reporting that its lush interiors might have been used to stand in for somewhere inside the Capitol.

    A former smelting factory complex in western Germany, Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord provides the backdrop for one of the most atmospheric settings in the films, Haymitch’s home of District 12. The vast complex is able to stand in for multiple places within the district, a former mining town that has fallen on seriously bad times. Rather than being a desolate area stumbled upon by the filmmakers, Landschaftspark is popular for its nightly light installation by British artist Jonathan Park. There are also regular al fresco events here, from film screenings to the annual art-meets-sport Ruhr Games and Traumzeit Festival. Another location in Germany, Lindlar Quarry, was used for District 12, with wooden huts built here to resemble the outskirts of the village.

    A version of this story originally appeared in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

    American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

    Recent findings suggest that seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom confirmed Friday.

    Seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

    “He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

    It has been revealed that jonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

    Industry observers note that gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

    It has been revealed that american will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A newly introduced reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be unveiled in December.

    According to recent reports, “For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

    The changes follow a broader management reshuffle confirmed in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

    American Airlines Officially Discontinues Boeing 777-300ER Flagship First Sales

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines stopped selling Flagship First on its Boeing 777-300ER fleet for travel on Thursday, ending the last long-haul international first-class product offered by a US airline.
    • Flagship Suites will replace both former premium cabins.
    • In a recent development, before the conversion, each aircraft carried eight Flagship First seats, 52 business seats, and 28 premium economy seats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines stopped selling Flagship First on its Boeing 777-300ER fleet for travel on Thursday, ending the last long-haul international first-class product offered by a US airline. The cutoff removes eight seats from every aircraft in the 20-jet fleet. American disclosed the date on September 2, the day its first retrofitted 777-300ER entered revenue service between Upcoming York-JFK and Buenos Aires. Business class is now the highest cabin customers can buy on the type.

    Flagship Suites will replace both former premium cabins. The retrofitted layout holds 70 lie-flat suites in a 1-2-1 arrangement, along with premium economy recliners and Main Cabin Extra seats, raising total capacity from 304 to 330. The aircraft, first delivered in 2012, was American’s only widebody with separate first and business cabins, and it serves long-haul routes from Miami, Dallas/Fort Worth, Los Angeles, Fresh York-JFK, and Charlotte to cities including London, Tokyo, São Paulo, and Sydney.

    In a recent development, before the conversion, each aircraft carried eight Flagship First seats, 52 business seats, and 28 premium economy seats. The first class cabin included private airport check-in and a dedicated fine dining experience at select airports. Under the new layout, all 70 passengers in the forward cabin receive identical service, including priority check-in, security, boarding, and baggage handling. Eight of the suites carry the Flagship Suite Preferred label, with up to 19% more bed space and 42% more living area than the standard suite, and Afar reports that they inherit features once reserved for first class.

    Boeing 777-300ER (Legacy Flagship).

    Boeing 777-300ER (Flagship Suites).

    In a recent development, the wider refresh benefits other passengers as well. Every seat now has a personal entertainment screen, a feature the old main cabin lacked, and AAdvantage members receive free WiFi sponsored by AT&T, which was previously sold separately. Bluetooth connectivity, 4K screens, and power are standard throughout. American also expanded Flagship Dining access to all Flagship customers, and lounge access remains available where offered.

    American is the last of the three largest network carriers to drop a separate international first class, following United and Delta, which gave up the cabin years ago. According to Fast Organization & Inc., all three have judged a standalone first cabin no longer worth the floor space it occupies. The move has been tied to carriers chasing higher-spending travelers, according to KSL.

    The seat math supports that reading. The Points Guy counted 60 lie-flat seats before the retrofit and 70 after, and premium economy grows from 28 to 44 seats. American says the result is more premium seats than any other US carrier operates on a single aircraft. United, the only other US operator of the 777-300ER, retrofitted its fleet in 2019 to hold up to 60 business class seats, leaving American with the larger premium cabin on the type.

    Industry observers note that transcontinental Flagship First follows on March 28, 2027, with the cutoff tied to more Airbus A321XLR aircraft entering the fleet. The A321 Transcon subfleet, which serves only Boston, Los Angeles, Fresh York, Orange County, and San Francisco, currently offers 10 first class and 20 business seats, and American has been converting those jets to a standard domestic first class layout. The A321XLR, by comparison, carries 20 Flagship Suites with 155 total seats.

    Industry observers note that on the widebody side, American prepares to retrofit all 20 777-300ERs by the end of 2027. The first aircraft, registered N718AN, spent eight months out of service in Hong Kong for its interior work, an indication of the scale of the program. The sources reviewed do not say how aircraft awaiting retrofit will be configured or sold after November 19, so travelers booking in the near term may want to confirm the cabin on their specific flight. Flagship Suites already fly on the 787-9 and the A321XLR, so the 777-300ER conversion carries the brand across three fleets. Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper called the aircraft “the next evolution of premium travel at American”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that senate Minority Leader Charles E.
    • According to recent reports, senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec.
    • That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    According to recent reports, senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

    That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

    The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

    It has been revealed that but supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

    “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

    Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

    “And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

    Several senators leaving the meeting stated the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

    That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

    With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

    According to recent reports, “No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., noted Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

    Industry observers note that “Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

    In a recent development, sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, mentioned, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

    “They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

    Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday noted at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

    “We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he mentioned. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

    According to recent reports, but there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

    “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., stated Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the latest ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

    In a recent development, several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve remarked many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

    Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

    Industry observers note that that included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

    Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

    Sources indicate that “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he remarked. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

    “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

    Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but stated, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

    “I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

    Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

    Recent findings suggest that senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

    “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan remarked.

    Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

    “We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

    “That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

    In a recent development, sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., mentioned, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

    Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

    “I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

    Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    The Best Hotels Near Disneyland Paris With Cinderella Suites, 'Toy Story'–Themed Rooms, and Quaint Cottages

    • According to recent reports, located just 40 minutes from Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport, Disneyland Paris is the ideal place to begin a Parisian vacation or say au revoir before returning home.

    • Of course, you'll need somewhere to rest your head at night, and that's where the best hotels near Disneyland Paris come into play.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, located just 40 minutes from Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport, Disneyland Paris is the ideal place to begin a Parisian vacation or say au revoir before returning home. Disneyland Paris's two theme parks, Disneyland Park and Disney Adventure World, pair timeless charm with an ease you'll never find stateside. Here, you can sip Champagne in front of Sleeping Beauty's castle—or visit a dragon beneath it—while filling your days with delightful architecture, unprecedented thrills, and the wildest wilderness ride Disney's ever built (Big Thunder Mountain!).

    There's also never been a better time to visit. Walt Disney Studios Park's March 2026 transformation into the newly introduced Disney Adventure World brought a drone-filled nighttime show, Avengers coaster, and even a Frozen-themed land featuring a lifelike Olaf robot to its once-faltering second gate. Now, between Fantasyland classics and futuristic favorites, there's something new and thrilling for the entire family to experience.

    Of course, you'll need somewhere to rest your head at night, and that's where the best hotels near Disneyland Paris come into play. Staying at a Disney-branded property typically affords guests special amenities including ticket packages, exclusive character meet-and-greets, and Extra Magic Time, which provides bonus time in the parks prior to opening. These hotels are great options, but can also be pricey—luckily, there are also a few non-branded properties in the area that make for great alternatives. There's something here for everyone and every budget.

    Sources indicate that unsure of whether you want to add something so Américain to your Paris vacation? As a theme park journalist who has visited all Disney parks worldwide, trust me: It's worth the visit. Even with so many cultural monuments in Paris, nothing is more delightfully uncanny than witnessing the United States section of It's a Small World. So, whether you're looking for glamour or simply a good location, read on for the very best hotels near Disneyland Paris.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: Three-minute walk.

    As the crown jewel of France's Disney resort, this 487-room property is Disney's best hotel overseas—and, quite possibly, in the entire world. After undergoing an extensive three-year overhaul, the iconic pink palace reopened in 2024 with princess suites and luxurious amenities worthy of its five-star ranking. Great for couples or families, guests can anticipate the ultimate royal treatment thanks to rooms with romantic castle views just steps from the park. With kids treatments at the Spa by Clarins and two complimentary hours of childcare each day, parents can unwind at the Fleur de Lys bar, enjoy a prix fixe meal at chef Jean Imbert's on-site restaurant, or perhaps even sneak back into the parks themselves. (We won't tell.).

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: Eight-minute drive.

    Recent findings suggest that rustic-chic in the best of ways, Marriott's Village d'Île-de-France offers cozy abodes that sleep up to eight with full kitchens, washing machines, and plenty of space to stretch out, all a short shuttle ride from the theme parks. Designed to emulate the charms of a small Parisian village, these quaint studios and multi-bedroom town houses feel more like cottages than traditional vacation rentals. Surroundings like these may sound quotidien to someone like Princess Belle, but the resort is as sweet as the rooms are spacious, making it an ideal choice for a hotel near Disneyland Paris as well as extended trips to nearby towns.

    Check Availability at Booking.com.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: 10-minute walk, 10-minute drive.

    Considering it's the only hotel in the world dedicated to Marvel's famed comic book characters, it's no surprise the Infinity Stone–colored beverages and slick, silver rooms at Disney Hotel New York - The Art of Marvel are somewhat out of this world. Family-friendly amenities like superhero meet-and-greets and a design studio with character drawing experiences make it the ultimate getaway for any comic book–obsessed fan in your family. Yet, even with hundreds of unique pieces of artwork, it won't feel like you're living through an Infinity War. Delicately executed details, like Manhattan Restaurant's Asgard-inspired chandelier and Spider-Man swinging across the panel screens at Skyline Bar, provide simple city elegance with the lightest touch of Marvel magic.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: 17-minute walk, 8-minute drive.

    If this hotel reminds you of Walt Disney World's Yacht & Beach Club resorts, you're not mistaken—this 1,098-room Disneyland Paris hotel was inspired by its Florida counterpart. The nautical theming is strong, and it's that seaside charm that keeps parkgoers returning to this waterfront escape. Just a 15-minute walk from the park gates, guests can meet maritime Mickey & Minnie Mouse (who don delightful cruisewear) or indulge in a seafood buffet at the aptly named Cape Cod restaurant. It's modeled after a familiar location back in the States, sure, but after spending the day with princesses, dragons, and superheroes, you may find yourself overjoyed to return to those country club comforts.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: 13-minute walk, 8-minute drive.

    Craving a bit more theming on your Disneyland Paris trip? Look no further than this national park–inspired escape. It offers lodge-style living perfect for a wintertime trip. Cozy up to the Redwood Bar & Lounge hearth, or in one of the newly renovated rooms with nods to Bambi and Pocahontas, and take in the charms of what Disney does best. Multiple on-site buffets allow you to feast like you've been on the move all day because, well, you likely have.

    Sources indicate that note that this Disney-operated hotel is right now undergoing a phased refurbishment. For stays in late 2026 and early 2027, I recommend selecting a refurbished room in The Lodges. Starting in February 2027, construction will move to general hotel spaces, and certain facilities will be temporarily unavailable.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: 30-minute walk, 10-minute drive.

    Rooms at the boutique Hôtel l’Elysée Val d’Europe are modern and minimal, offering the perfect escape from any theme park chaos. Though it's just a 30-minute walk or a short, free shuttle ride away from the gates, the real perk of being a bit removed is its proximity to the Val d’Europe shopping complex and the designer outlet mall La Vallée Village. With a bounty of discounted prices on luxury brands like Prada, Saint Laurent, and Gucci, you're sure to find a Parisian souvenir that'll rival the array of Mickey Mouse goods sold within the parks.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: Nine-minute drive.

    In a recent development, if the City of Lights appeals to you for its style and romance, consider this your ideal hotel. Design-forward rooms with concrete walls, sleek bathrooms, and an open, plant-walled lobby offer reliable value without sacrificing taste, making it a perfect choice for travelers seeking something a little less Disney. While families will benefit from select rooms offering full kitchens and stovetops, the upgraded amenities—which include a heated indoor pool, sauna, and hammam—offer a little something for everyone, just beyond the parks.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: 16-minute walk, 10-minute drive.

    Step right up to this quirky hotel that feels like a Western film set and is jam-packed with Toy Story details. Small touches, like cowprint bedspreads and appearances by Woody and Jessie, make Disney Hotel Cheyenne a hidden gem that's nearly as themed as Disneyland Paris's own Frontierland. Given that it's significantly more affordable than the majority of its Disneyland-owned counterparts yet retains perks like Extra Magic Time, this property offers a best-of-both-worlds approach for those who want to live a full Disney-fied day from first rides to fireworks.

    Distance from Disneyland Paris: 10-minute drive.

    Multi-room cabins at this expansive, woodsy resort are the perfect way to experience a taste of the outdoors between trips on Significant Thunder Mountain. Sadly, there are no theme park shuttle services, so parks must be reached by car, rideshare, or taxi. But that's not to say it's worth skipping—here, nature abounds in both form and function. There's an on-site aviary, comfort food at the Crockett's Tavern buffet, and plenty of rustic charm, so the comforts of home are never too far away. Consider this Disneyland Paris hotel as close as you can get to camping at Disneyland's theme parks—if camping also included unfettered access to Mickey waffles.

    What area is the best to stay in when visiting Disneyland Paris?

    Recent findings suggest that any hotel near Disney Village, the entertainment and dining district at the entrance to Disneyland Paris's two theme parks, is going to be the most convenient choice. This not only offers more ease and access, but affords you the option to shop and dine after the parks close each night. Still, booking nearly any Disney-operated hotel will give you benefits like Extra Magic Time and exclusive character encounters, which help get you even more out of your Disneyland Paris vacation.

    Are there any hotels that are walking distance to Disneyland Paris?

    Industry observers note that yes—but you might want to bring your sneakers. Disneyland Hotel is located directly at the entrance to Disneyland Paris, while Disney Hotel Upcoming York - The Art of Marvel, Disney Newport Bay Club, and Disney Sequoia Lodge are all a 10- to 15-minute walk through Disney Village to reach both parks. Disney Hotel Cheyenne is a further trek, about 15 to 20 minutes away, but absolutely doable. Shuttle buses are available as well.

    What is the 3-2-1 rule at Disneyland Paris?

    In a recent development, the 3-2-1 rule is essentially shorthand for how to streamline your Disneyland Paris experience. Experts recommend selecting three rides, two entertainment offerings, and one dining option for an easy, straightforward approach to planning a day at any Disney theme park. It works as well at Walt Disney World and Disneyland as it does here at Disneyland Paris, but I recommend you still do a little research before you go. Be sure you don't skip Phantom Manor, which can only be found in Paris, secure your dining reservations early, and don't miss the nighttime demonstrates offered at both parks—they're among the best in the world.

    It is best to stay within the park at Disneyland Paris, or outside of it?

    It goes without saying that the closer you are to the castle, the “better” your hotel will be, but it shouldn't be a deal-breaker. Convenience is always a factor, but Disney-operated hotels at Disneyland Paris tend to be much pricier than their American counterparts, so staying a bus ride away might be necessary. Still, the perks are plenty across most of Disneyland's own hotels, including extra time in the parks, which is why I recommended so many of them.

    #19625. Why Long-Haul Flights Carry 3 Or 4 Pilots & How Airbus Wants To Cut Some To 2

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1474 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Long-Haul Flights Carry 3 Or 4 Pilots & How Airbus Wants To Cut Some To 2

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1474 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Essentially, all commercial airliners in service today need two pilots: one captain and a first officer.
    • This is done on long-haul and ultra-long-haul flights because crew rest regulations allow each pilot to work only a limited number of hours each day.
    • Exact practices vary by local regulations and sometimes by standard airline operating procedures.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Essentially, all commercial airliners in service today need two pilots: one captain and a first officer. These two have always been present on large transport aircraft, but airliners of the past also included a flight engineer, with earlier models even having a dedicated navigator and radio operator. However, as technology advanced and more aircraft functions were automated, manufacturers trimmed down flight crews until today, when most flights require only two pilots. Still, many widebody flights operate with three or four pilots, as one or two pilots may serve as a relief pilot.

    This is done on long-haul and ultra-long-haul flights because crew rest regulations allow each pilot to work only a limited number of hours each day. The larger roster allows pilots to rotate throughout the flight, with one or two resting onboard. This arrangement ensures compliance with regulations and preserves safety, but it's also expensive. As such, some airlines and Airbus are looking to change it.

    Exact practices vary by local regulations and sometimes by standard airline operating procedures. Generally, however, the rule of thumb is that any flight over eight hours requires a third pilot to be rostered, while flights scheduled to exceed 12 hours must be staffed with four pilots. All crew members will be present in the flight deck during critical phases of flight.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, during cruise, they will rotate among each other so that two crew members are flying while the third (and fourth, if applicable) are resting. Some carriers will roster the relief pilot as either another first officer or captain, while others may specifically roster 'second officers' (also known as cruise pilots) who do not perform takeoffs or landings.

    Typical Pilot Crew Rest Facilities.

    Located on passenger deck behind flight deck, or.

    underfloor modules located within the cargo hold, or.

    Overhead modules located in the crown area.

    Located on passenger deck behind flight deck.

    Located on passenger deck behind flight deck.

    Underfloor modules located within the cargo hold, or.

    Overhead modules located in the crown area (newer) or.

    underfloor modules located within the cargo hold, or.

    Overhead modules located in the crown area.

    Overhead modules located in the crown area.

    On the world's longest flights, carriers will typically staff flights with two of their most senior captains and two of their most senior first officers, while carriers that roster second officers will not schedule them on their longest services. The actual onboard rest schedule is typically determined by the pilots themselves, developed in such a way to ensure compliance with the airline's home regulator. Onboard, most modern widebody aircraft are equipped with crew rest pods located either above or below the passenger cabin, featuring two beds as well as a seat. These are often, but not always, separate from the flight attendant crew rest area, while aircraft that do not include a dedicated rest area instead have blocked business class seats for pilots.

    In a recent development, most airline pilots are paid by the hour, which means that crew costs increase the longer a flight is. In addition, longer services require an extra pilot or two, which can nearly double pilot salary costs on an ultra-long-haul service. When taking into account that most long-haul flights are performed by widebody aircraft, this further increases crew costs.

    In a recent development, after all, widebodies pay more than a narrowbody aircraft type, resulting in extremely high labor costs for a 12, 13, or 15-hour flight using large twin-aisle jets. Long-haul and ultra-long-haul flights are quite challenging economically due to added fuel costs, overflight fees, and staffing costs. Augmented crews typically no longer require blocked seats due to the widespread use of underfloor or crown-area rest pods.

    In a recent development, however, the costs of rostering a captain and three first officers or two captains and two first officers on their own are immense. This is especially true when considering that pilots who regularly operate ultra-long-haul services are typically an airline's most senior and best-paid crew members. The airline industry is infamously cost-sensitive, and ultra-long-haul flights are the most difficult for an airline to make money on.

    Industry observers note that this is despite the revenue premium that they typically command. Airlines, already constantly hunting for ways to reduce operating costs, have also been turning to pilots for more savings, particularly on widebody ultra-long-haul flights. For its part, Airbus has been working on systems to eliminate the need for augmented crews on the A350, which includes the ability to cruise with just one crew member at the controls.

    Industry observers note that airbus has been working on developing systems to enable extended Minimum Crew Operations (eMCO) for the A350. With this system, the aircraft still requires two pilots for takeoffs and landings, but one crew member would rest during cruise while the other would be present at the controls. The two would then rotate throughout the flight, with only one pilot actively flying at a time.

    It has been revealed that airbus's role would be to redesign cockpit displays and modify systems to reduce workload on the pilot. It has been working with airlines such as Cathay Pacific and Lufthansa to evaluate the feasibility of eMCO, while also working with EASA to assess whether the concept compromises safety.

    In a recent development, the agency launched a proposal in 2022, which was sent to ICAO, and aimed to potentially transition to eMCO operations as early as 2027. This could allow airlines to significantly cut crew costs for long-haul flights while also reducing the impact of the widely reported pilot shortage. Airbus has been discussing with customers implementing this potential new feature throughout the A350 family.

    It has also been looking at potentially implementing the technology in the upcoming A350F, which is set to enter service in 2027. While Airbus has been pushing for the development of eMCO procedures, Boeing has stated that the technology isn't yet in place for single-pilot cruise operations to be executed safely. What's more, while there was momentum for Airbus's eMCO initiative, this has since faded.

    According to recent reports, in February 2026, the US Congress passed a new law requiring two pilots to be present at all times in the flight deck on all commercial airline flights. While this was previously enforced by FAA regulations, the new legislation codifies this into law, essentially closing any pathways for airlines and manufacturers to push for single-pilot operations.

    It has been revealed that while it wouldn't be impossible for this law to be undone, it's much more difficult to change the law than to amend FAA regulations. EASA has paused and shelved its research on eMCO and single-pilot operations, concluding that implementing such practices would reduce safety.

    According to recent reports, the regulator was particularly concerned about fatigue management, meeting a pilot's physiological needs, and cross-checking between crew members. As such, it ruled out any regulatory changes in the near future. Instead, the focus is on improving cockpit technologies rather than reducing the number of pilots in the flight deck.

    Industry observers note that while it's often been discussed that airline flight crews have shrunk throughout history, what is often overlooked is that not everyone performs the same function. Flight engineers, navigators, and radio operators all served distinct roles, while there were always two pilots who primarily flew the aircraft. The functions formerly handled by flight engineers, navigators, and radio operators have either been automated or are now handled by the pilots.

    Recent findings suggest that regulators have rejected single-pilot operations on commercial transport aircraft. EASA has shelved any aims to operate airliners with one pilot at any time, while the US has prohibited this by law. What's more, existing single-pilot aircraft remain under scrutiny, as the FAA has recently rescinded single-pilot operation exemptions for several Cessna Citation models.

    This was due to increased accident rates, reportedly double compared with two-pilot flights, along with widespread compliance failures. At the same time, pilots are expensive, and the airline industry is particularly cost-sensitive, which makes developments that cut down on crew costs quite lucrative to airlines. In addition to initiatives like Airbus's work on eMCO for the A350, Merlin is working on developing newly introduced AI-assisted copilot systems that could be installed on essentially any large airliner. While these systems are meant to assist pilots at first, the long-term goal is to enable single-pilot or fully autonomous operations.

    The burden on Airbus or Merlin is to prove that their proposals materially enhance safety compared to today's system of mandating at least two pilots during a flight. Thus far, they have failed to prove this, which means that these systems cannot be implemented in their intended form in the near future. What will happen in the distant future is unclear, but regulators have a responsibility to maintain and enhance safety in aviation, first and foremost.

    #19624. Breaking: Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (773 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, former Alaska Rep.
    • In a recent development, former Rep.
    • The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

    In a recent development, former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

    The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

    With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

    “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola noted in a statement after the race was called.

    Sources indicate that the Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

    Industry observers note that peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

    She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

    She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

    But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The Fresh York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

    Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

    According to recent reports, prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

    According to recent reports, trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

    The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

    But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

    "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

    Sources indicate that in other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

    The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

    Industry News: Livery of the Week: Iberia’s Red-and-Yellow Design

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (548 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Airlinegeeks

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
